h1: 10 Best Things to Do in Uttaradit
intro: Uttaradit is a small town on the border of the lower north that hides more good stuff than you'd expect — a hero's monument right in the town centre, the town of Laplae with its legend of the widows, Thailand's largest earthen dam, and even the largest teak tree in the world. We've rounded up the 10 attractions real visitors talk about most, with admission fees, locations, and trip-planning tips, whether you're doing a single day in town or driving out to the dam and Nam Pat for an overnight trip.

blocks.html:
Uttaradit's charm is that it's a "pass-through town you fall for once you stop and look." The town centre clusters around the provincial hall, with the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument standing proud as the first stop everyone makes. About ten-odd kilometres west lies Laplae, a valley town with the legend of the widows and its "no-lying zone," complete with a city gate arching over the road, old wooden houses, and ancient temples tucked at the foot of the hills. Head out of town toward Tha Pla and Nam Pat and you'll find nature in full force — the crest of Sirikit Dam with mountains rippling against a vast reservoir, and forest holding thousand-year-old giant teak trees. There's plenty to string together, whether you're into temple visits and merit-making, old-town wandering, nature, or just chilling at a cafe.

This list includes the spots you shouldn't skip when you come to Uttaradit — like the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument, honouring Uttaradit's hero, with a museum of giant Nam Phi steel swords right behind it to explore further; Wat Phra Thaen Sila At, a royal temple on Turtle Hill with a sacred stone platform revered across the upper north; Sirikit Dam, Thailand's largest earthen dam, with sunset views so good people plan their visit around them; Ton Sak Yai National Park, home to the largest teak tree in the world at over a thousand years old; and the Bo Lek Nam Phi iron mines, birthplace of the Nam Phi steel sword legend, where you can try panning for iron to keep as a lucky charm. For old-town and shopping fans, there's the Laplae City Museum, Wat Don Sak with one of the province's most beautifully carved wooden temple doors, Uttaradit Walking Street along the irrigation canal, and a garden cafe on the Phichai side called CAFE' De FIELD. Scroll through each spot below and plan your own route.

blocks.name: Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument
blocks.area: In front of Uttaradit Provincial Hall, Tha It Subdistrict, Mueang Uttaradit District
blocks.signature: A monument to Uttaradit's hero standing proud in front of the provincial hall, with the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Museum and a giant Nam Phi steel sword museum right behind it to explore further. The first stop everyone visiting Uttaradit makes.
blocks.descHtml:
If you land in Uttaradit and aren't sure where to start, this is the answer. The Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument stands proud in front of the provincial hall, serving almost as the face of the town — everyone stops here for the first photo of their trip. The statue depicts him seated as ruler of Phichai, right hand gripping a sword broken into two pieces, symbolising his heroics fighting the Burmese in 1773, when his sword broke but he fought on to victory anyway. It suits history buffs, families teaching their kids, and anyone wanting to tick off the province's landmark.

What makes this spot worth more than just a photo with a statue is that behind the monument sit two museums you can walk straight into: the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Museum, which tells his story through displayed weapons, battle dioramas, and commemorative coins, and the Nam Phi Steel Sword Museum, which displays a giant sword. Nam Phi steel is Uttaradit's famous high-grade steel, used to forge weapons since ancient times. Some foreign visitors have even called it one of the best-curated museums they've seen in Thailand — and best of all, both are free to enter.

Costs are painless — the monument plaza is open around the clock for paying respects, no entry fee. The museums behind it open roughly 09:00–16:00 daily, also free. There's ample parking on both the sports-field side and the provincial-administration side, and the location sits right in the town centre, easy to reach near the provincial hall and government district.

One small heads-up from past visitors: the plaza itself is an open space in full sun, and midday gets quite hot with little shade. It's better to come in the morning or late afternoon, then head into the air-conditioned museums. Plan it well and you can knock the whole visit out in about an hour, walking away with both nice photos and a slice of the town's history.
mustOrder: Photograph the seated Phraya Phichai statue, sword broken into two pieces in his right hand
Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Museum behind the monument (free entry)
Nam Phi Steel Sword Museum — view the largest sword on display
Visit in the morning or evening — midday sun is intense
blocks.bestFor: The first stop of any Uttaradit trip — pay respects, then tour the museums
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Oatz / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

blocks.name: Laplae City Gate (Laplae Widow Monument)
blocks.area: Highway 1041, Si Phanom Mat Subdistrict, Laplae District, Uttaradit
blocks.signature: An arched gate in applied Sukhothai style straddling the road into Laplae. Beside it stands the Widow Monument — a woman cradling her child with her downcast husband nearby, inscribed 'Only your word of truth,' referencing the legend of the town of widows. A photo stop everyone makes before entering town.
blocks.descHtml:
Drive from downtown Uttaradit toward Laplae District for about 8 kilometres and you'll soon reach the "Laplae City Gate," a large golden-yellow arch straddling Highway 1041, standing tall as the official welcome gate into Laplae. The gate itself is a piece of applied Sukhothai-style art, 10 metres wide and 41 metres long, designed by the Fine Arts Department — visible from a distance, so you know you've arrived the moment you see it. It's a spot almost everyone stops to photograph before entering town. If you like collecting town landmarks or are on a northern road trip, this is the first stop not to drive past.

The highlight everyone talks about is the Widow Monument standing beside the gate — a statue of a young woman cradling her infant with a sad expression, beside her a husband standing with downcast shoulders, carrying a bag of turmeric. The base is inscribed with the words "Only your word of truth," referencing the legend of Laplae, said to be a town where lying is forbidden. Young Laplae women could marry men from elsewhere on the condition that they never lie; the moment a husband slipped up and told a lie, he had to leave town, leaving her a widow. That's the origin of the nickname "Laplae, town of widows." This small statue carries a story that keeps many visitors standing and reading for a while.

Costs are painless — it's free to visit, no entry fee, and you can park along the roadside. The gate is open for photos around the clock. Some reviewers say it's lit up beautifully in the evening. If you come during the day, be ready for harsh sunlight and roadside parking with constant passing traffic. Across from the gate sits the Laplae City Museum, also free, open 09:00–16:00 — worth walking over to if you want to dig deeper into the town's story.

This spot is popular because it's both the mandatory check-in point for anyone visiting Laplae and a single symbol that tells the town's whole identity. One small thing to know: it's more of a quick photo stop than a place for a long stroll — 15–20 minutes is plenty — then drive on into Laplae itself to see the market, the Chao Fa Ham Kuman Monument, and the district's famous durian orchards.
mustOrder: Photograph the golden applied-Sukhothai-style gate straddling the road
The Widow Monument — a mother cradling her child beside her downcast husband, inscribed 'Only your word of truth'
Hear the legend of the no-lying town, Laplae the town of widows
Walk over to the Laplae City Museum across the road (free)
blocks.bestFor: First photo stop before entering Laplae — a quick break mid-road-trip
blocks.hours: Open 24 hours daily (museum across the road: 09:00–16:00)
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Tevaprapas / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

blocks.name: Wat Phra Thaen Sila At Royal Temple
blocks.area: Thung Yang Subdistrict, Laplae District, Uttaradit
blocks.signature: An ancient royal temple on Turtle Hill, home to a sacred stone platform believed to have been visited by five Buddhas. Revered across the upper north, with an annual worship festival during Makha Bucha.
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Phra Thaen Sila At Royal Temple is one of Uttaradit's oldest temples, sitting on Turtle Hill in Thung Yang Subdistrict, Laplae District. Originally called Wat Mahathat, it's believed to date back to the Sukhothai period and has since been elevated to a third-class royal temple under the Thammayut order. It's ideal for those wanting to make merit and pray, temple enthusiasts drawn to old legends, and families who want to bring elders along for an easy, unhurried visit.

The must-see highlight is the "Phra Thaen Sila At" — a rectangular laterite stone slab with a lotus-petal-carved base, enshrined in the temple hall atop the hill. It's long been believed that all five Buddhas of this auspicious era once sat here in meditation, making it a site of deep reverence across the upper north. Another popular photo spot is the temple hall's old carved wooden doors, plus a local museum inside the temple grounds housing ancient artefacts. Nearby, on the same hill, stands Wat Phra Yeun Phutthabat Yuklon, an easy add-on visit.

Genuine reviews consistently describe the temple as shaded, leafy, and well laid out, with a calm, cool atmosphere befitting an ancient site. Entry is free, no admission fee, open daily roughly 08:00–17:00. It sits about 5–6 kilometres from downtown Uttaradit, under ten minutes by car, with convenient parking.

What makes this temple so well loved is the annual Phra Thaen Sila At worship festival held during Makha Bucha (the full moon of the third lunar month), which draws crowds from in and out of province. Worth knowing: it's a hillside temple, so dress modestly, remove your shoes before entering the hall, and if you'd rather avoid the crowds, visit on a weekday for a more peaceful atmosphere.
mustOrder: Phra Thaen Sila At — the laterite platform with a lotus-petal-carved base inside the temple hall
The old carved wooden doors of the temple hall
The local museum within the temple grounds
The Phra Thaen worship festival during Makha Bucha
blocks.bestFor: Temple visits and merit-making, viewing an old temple with family or elders
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Takeaway / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

blocks.name: Sirikit Dam
blocks.signature: Thailand's largest earthen dam, with dam-crest views over a maze of mountains against a vast reservoir. A great sunset spot, with bicycles for hire across the dam crest, plus a cafe and grilled-fish stalls by the water.
blocks.descHtml:
Sirikit Dam is Thailand's largest earthen dam, damming the Nan River in Pha Lueat Subdistrict, Tha Pla District, about 60 kilometres from downtown Uttaradit. If you like quiet nature, mountain views, and a reservoir stretching as far as the eye can see, this is a great fit. Drive up onto the dam crest and you'll see views on both sides — one a still lake backed by a maze of mountains, the other a valley below. Most reviews agree the atmosphere is peaceful, the air cool, and the grounds clean and well maintained — more a family retreat than a bustling tourist hub.

The must-do is standing on the dam crest to take in the view, especially in the evening as the sun sets behind the mountain ridge — many say it's the most beautiful photo spot in Uttaradit. There's also a bike-rental point for riding across the dam crest (around 20 baht per hour), a suspension bridge over the river, a viewing pavilion, and a Buddha image to pay respects to. Near the dam sit a cafe and riverside restaurants known for grilled fish and other fresh dishes straight from the reservoir — a relaxed spot to eat while taking in the view.

Another plus: it's free to enter, no admission fee. Your real budget is just fuel, bike rental, and food. It's open daily during daytime hours; come in the morning or evening to avoid the harshest midday sun. Worth knowing: there's no public transport here, so you'll need your own car or a rental, and the grounds are fairly spacious — allow half a day to wander without rushing. It's a worthwhile stop if you want to see another side of Uttaradit beyond the town itself.
mustOrder: View the dam crest and sunset
Rent a bicycle to ride across the dam crest
Grilled-fish restaurants by the reservoir
The suspension bridge over the river
blocks.bestFor: Evening views and sunset with family
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Takeaway / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

blocks.name: Laplae City Museum
blocks.area: Si Phanom Mat Subdistrict, Laplae District, Uttaradit
blocks.signature: A museum of wooden houses recreating traditional Laplae life, telling the legend of the widow town and its 'no-lying zone.' Free entry, spacious shaded lawn, with traditional sweets sold nearby.
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to make the most of visiting Laplae, locals will tell you to stop at the "Laplae City Museum" first, because it's the place that tells you the town's whole legend before you go exploring for real. It sits right beside the Laplae City Gate on Injaimee Road, Si Phanom Mat Subdistrict, only about 5–8 kilometres out from downtown Uttaradit — under twenty minutes by car. It's a great fit for first-time visitors to Laplae, families teaching kids, and anyone who loves capturing old-town corners.

The highlight is a raised wooden house recreating traditional Laplae life — walk up into it and you're transported back in time, with a cotton spinner, a teen-jok weaving loom, and a kitchen displaying local food like mee pan (Laplae's noodle wraps). Many reviewers love the "simulated cave telling the legend of the town" — step inside and it's cool with air conditioning, where you can read about the town of widows and its trademark "no lying" rule. Out front stands a statue of a widow cradling her child beside her husband holding a bag of turmeric, about to leave town — a paired landmark photo spot everyone captures.

On atmosphere, reviewers agree the museum isn't huge — a comfortable stroll of about an hour — with a spacious, shaded lawn and frangipani arbours for plenty of photos. The best part is free entry, no admission fee, with parking available, and a stall selling traditional sweets and local goods nearby. Open daily roughly 09:00–16:00 (sometimes later during festivals).

Worth knowing: this is a community learning centre, so most signage is in Thai — non-Thai speakers may need to rely on the visuals — and some reviews note the restrooms could be cleaner. Overall, though, it's a great starting point for a Laplae trip, delivering legend, way of life, and beautiful photo spots without spending a single baht.
mustOrder: The Laplae City Gate and the widow-and-child statue at the entrance (paired town-landmark photo)
The wooden house recreating traditional Laplae life — cotton spinner, teen-jok weaving loom, kitchen
The simulated cave telling the legend of the widow town and its no-lying rule (cool and air-conditioned)
The frangipani arbour and spacious shaded lawn around the museum
blocks.bestFor: First-time visit to Laplae, wanting to learn the legend before exploring town + families teaching kids
blocks.zone: Laplae town (~5-8 km from downtown Uttaradit)

blocks.title: 🛏️ Where to Stay in Uttaradit — Sleep in Town for Easy Access to Laplae and the Dam
blocks.text: To make the most of an Uttaradit trip, try staying a night so you can split it into two unhurried days. Day one covers the town and Laplae; day two drives up to Sirikit Dam and the giant teak tree. Popular hotels cluster in downtown Uttaradit, near the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument, the walking street, and the road out to Laplae, with both in-town hotels and small budget-friendly guesthouses. Pick a location close to whatever you want to see first thing in the morning for the best value — compare prices and reviews across a few sites before booking.

blocks.name: Bo Lek Nam Phi Iron Mines (Bo Lek Nam Phi Museum)
blocks.area: Nam Phi Subdistrict, Thong Saen Khan District, Uttaradit
blocks.signature: An ancient high-grade iron ore deposit tied to the legend of the Nam Phi steel sword. Try panning for iron at the Royal Sword and Royal Blade pits to keep as a lucky charm, alongside a museum explaining the smelting and forging process. Free entry.
blocks.priceRange: Free (paid only if you buy amulets)
blocks.descHtml:
If you like attractions steeped in legend, the Bo Lek Nam Phi iron mines (Bo Lek Nam Phi Museum) in Nam Phi Subdistrict, Thong Saen Khan District, is a one-of-a-kind stop. This is a natural high-grade iron ore deposit long said to have supplied the raw material for royal swords. Nam Phi steel is famed for its strength, resilience, and rust resistance, and spiritually inclined visitors believe it carries a sacredness of its own. It's a great fit for anyone wanting both historical knowledge and a spiritually auspicious experience in a single trip, and works well for families or those seeking blessings.

The highlight nobody misses is the Royal Sword pit and Royal Blade pit — two pits once reserved exclusively for kings. The fun part: staff provide a bamboo rod fitted with a magnet so you can try fishing iron ore up from the pit; once you've caught some, take it home as a lucky charm. Kids love it. Nearby stands a shrine to the guardian spirit of the Bo Lek Nam Phi mines, worth stopping to pray at, while inside the museum building, dioramas walk you through the whole process, from mining ore to smelting to forging it into a sword — making it easy to picture how a lump of iron becomes a weapon.

Budget-wise, it's painless — entry is free, with the only cost being amulets if you want to buy some. Out front, a community-enterprise shop sells pressed Nam Phi iron bars, amulets, swords, and other iron-themed souvenirs, at a range of price points. The museum is open daily 08:00–17:00. It sits about 56 kilometres from downtown Uttaradit, reached via Highway 11 then Route 1245, with convenient parking.

This spot is popular because it's the "one and only" iron mine tied to the Nam Phi sword legend and beliefs around fortune and protection, drawing both the spiritually minded and history buffs alike. Worth knowing: it's a small local museum focused narrowly on iron and legend, not a large-scale museum. If you make it out this way, it's a worthwhile stop, offering knowledge, lucky charms, and an iron-panning experience you won't find anywhere else.
mustOrder: Pan for iron ore with a magnet at the Royal Sword and Royal Blade pits to keep as a charm
Pay respects at the shrine to the guardian spirit of the Bo Lek Nam Phi mines
View the diorama of the smelting and forging process in the museum
Shop for pressed Nam Phi iron bars / amulets at the community-enterprise store
blocks.bestFor: Praying for blessings and collecting lucky charms, plus families wanting a historical trip
blocks.zone: Nam Phi Subdistrict, Thong Saen Khan District
blocks.libCredit: Photo by เทวประภาส มากคล้าย (Tevaprapas) / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

blocks.name: Ton Sak Yai National Park
blocks.area: Moo 4, Ban Pang Kluea, Nam Khrai Subdistrict, Nam Pat District, Uttaradit
blocks.signature: Home to the largest teak tree in the world, over 1,000 years old, with a trunk that takes many arm-spans to encircle and a height of around 40 metres. Walk through shaded forest with rest pavilions along the way, and pair it with a visit to Sirikit Dam.
blocks.priceRange: Free (park fee: adults 20 baht, children 10 baht)
blocks.descHtml:
If you enjoy quiet nature and want to see something you can't find anywhere else, "Ton Sak Yai National Park" in Nam Pat District, Uttaradit, is a stop worth making. The draw is right there in the name — this is home to the largest living teak tree in the world. Locals call it Ton Sak Mahesak. Its trunk measures nearly ten metres around (roughly 9.85 metres, requiring many arm-spans to encircle), standing about 40–47 metres tall, estimated to be at least a thousand years old, possibly as old as 1,500 years — towering in the forest and recognised as one of Thailand's wonder trees.

Once there, the main highlight is walking in to see the giant teak tree, via a shaded nature trail with plenty of tree cover for a cool, comfortable walk, plus a pavilion where you can sit and photograph the tree in comfort. Most reviews agree the atmosphere is quiet and uncrowded, ideal for a relaxed stroll and fresh air. Anyone with more time can explore Huai Niam Waterfall, Mon Kaeo Waterfall, and caves like Tham Chan and Tham Chedi within the park, plus the summit of Doi Phu Miang for serious hikers.

Costs are very easy on the wallet — many sources note free entry, though some periods charge a park fee of 20 baht for adults and 10 baht for children. There's ample parking, and it's open roughly 08:30–18:00. It's located in Ban Pang Kluea, Nam Khrai Subdistrict, reached via Highway 1047. A key advantage is that you can pair it with Sirikit Dam in a single trip since they sit along the same route.

Worth knowing: this spot is set deep in Nam Pat District, and the final stretch is a winding mountain road, so check your car's condition and fill up on fuel beforehand — phone signal can be patchy in places. It's best to come in the morning through early afternoon so you have time to walk the trail and see other spots in the park. Wear comfortable walking shoes and bring mosquito repellent for a more enjoyable visit.
mustOrder: The largest teak tree in the world — trunk 9.85 metres around, roughly 47 metres tall, over 1,000 years old
Walk the shaded nature trail through the forest
Huai Niam and Mon Kaeo waterfalls, plus caves within the park
Rest at the pavilion by the giant teak tree, then continue on to Sirikit Dam
blocks.bestFor: Nature lovers hiking to see the giant teak tree, pairing with a trip to Sirikit Dam
blocks.zone: Nam Pat District (route up to Sirikit Dam-Nam Pat)
blocks.libCredit: Photo by เทวประภาส มากคล้าย / Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)

blocks.name: Wat Don Sak
blocks.area: 15/2 Moo 12, Fai Luang Subdistrict, Laplae District, Uttaradit
blocks.signature: An old temple with carved wooden hall doors bearing curling kanok-vine motifs from the late Ayutthaya period. The left and right panels differ in pattern yet fit together seamlessly when closed — one of the province's most beautifully carved door pairs.
blocks.descHtml:
If you love antiques with a story behind them, Wat Don Sak in Ban Fai Luang, Laplae District, is a spot that art-history fans say you shouldn't drive past. The temple sits about 9 kilometres from downtown Uttaradit toward Laplae, believed to date to the late Ayutthaya period. Its name, "Don Sak," comes from a story that the original hall was built from a single large teak tree growing naturally on a mound. It's a great fit for anyone wanting a more substantive visit to Laplae, rather than just a photo check-in.

The highlight everyone talks about is the pair of carved wooden hall doors — a master-craft piece considered one of the three most beautiful Buddhist temple door pairs in the province. The doors are carved entirely in curling kanok-vine motifs, with mythical Himmapan creatures woven gracefully into the pattern, while the door frames carry alternating foreign-kanok and crab-claw-kanok motifs. What amazes visitors is that the left and right panels are carved in completely different patterns, yet when the doors close, the patterns line up seamlessly — a striking testament to Ayutthaya-era craftsmanship. Wood-carving fans should take their time standing close to appreciate it.

The overall atmosphere is quiet, like an uncrowded countryside temple. Visitor reviews consistently note a peaceful mood and an easy, unhurried stroll. Entry is free, with parking available, open roughly 08:00–17:30. Come mid-morning to early afternoon for enough light to appreciate the door details, since the doors themselves are quite old and some angles are dim.

Worth knowing: this temple is a cultural attraction that doesn't yet have many reviews on travel platforms. Most visitors are art lovers or people who've already read up on Laplae's history, so don't expect many shops or amenities. Treat it as a stop along a Laplae trip — pair it with the Laplae City Museum or the old-town monuments — and it'll be well worth the drive. Dress modestly and be respectful per temple etiquette.
mustOrder: The pair of carved wooden hall doors with curling kanok-vine motifs from the late Ayutthaya period — different patterns on each side, seamless when closed
The old teak hall, said to be built entirely from a single teak tree on the mound
The door frames' alternating foreign-kanok and crab-claw-kanok motifs, with Himmapan creatures woven into the pattern
Historical traces of the temple's story of surviving the Burmese war
blocks.bestFor: Art and ancient architecture fans + a stop while touring Laplae
blocks.zone: Ban Fai Luang, Laplae District (west edge of town)
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Panupong Roopyai / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

blocks.name: Uttaradit Walking Street
blocks.signature: Uttaradit locals' weekend walking street, selling savoury and sweet food, snacks, and handmade/homemade goods. A relaxed evening stroll along the irrigation canal.
blocks.descHtml:
If your Uttaradit visit happens to land on a Saturday evening, don't miss Uttaradit Walking Street. This is the town's regular weekend evening market, running along the road beside the irrigation canal next to Uttaradit Rajabhat University, stretching roughly from the Injaimee intersection to the Centenary Bridge. It's perfect for anyone who wants to stroll and snack without much planning — just wander and stop whenever something looks good. It's a free attraction that families, couples, or solo travellers can all enjoy.

The highlight here is the rotating local food stalls — savoury dishes, sweets, fried and grilled snacks, smoothies, milk tea, plus all kinds of treats and snacks lining both sides of the street. Beyond food, there's also a zone of handmade and homemade goods, craft work, jewellery, and locally made ideas. Some weeks feature special activities like a "one district, one creative space" event or small performances to enjoy while you stroll. Visitors consistently describe it as lively, packed with stalls, and busy with crowds — a fun place to walk and eat.

What sets this apart from a typical walking street is the canal-side view — walking here in the evening light with a cool breeze makes for a comfortable atmosphere. Regulars recommend coming around 17:00–19:00, when all the stalls are open, crowds are building, and the light is still good for photos. Food prices are affordable — a real eating budget of around ฿100–200 will leave you full and happy, with free entry, no admission fee.

Worth knowing: the walking street runs only on Saturday evenings, roughly 16:00–21:00 (it used to run on Sundays in the past, but is now fixed to Saturdays per the official page) — check the page beforehand in case it's cancelled or rescheduled for a festival. Parking is available along the road near the university; when it's busy you may need to walk a bit further, but it's a fair trade for a genuinely local canal-side evening market experience.
mustOrder: Local Uttaradit food, savoury and sweet, rotating by stall
Fried and grilled snacks, smoothies, milk tea — grazing as you go
Local handmade/homemade craft goods
Stroll along the irrigation canal in the evening light, around 17:00–19:00
blocks.bestFor: A relaxed evening stroll and snack along the canal on a Saturday

blocks.name: CAFE' De FIELD
blocks.area: 79/8 Moo 1, Kho Rum Subdistrict, Phichai District, Uttaradit 53120
blocks.signature: A large-house cafe set amid a lawn and landscaped garden, with plenty of outdoor photo spots. Serves coffee, one-plate dishes, spaghetti, and a range of desserts — a relaxed photo-friendly cafe on the Phichai side.
blocks.descHtml:
If you're on the Phichai side and want a relaxed, photo-worthy cafe, locals often point to "CAFE' De FIELD," which many affectionately call the Cafe De Field. It's a large white house set amid a lawn and landscaped garden that wraps around the front, side, and back of the building, sitting just off the road before the traffic light into Phichai town — easy to find, with comfortable parking. It suits cafe lovers who like leafy green corners, visitors passing through Phichai wanting a coffee break, and families letting kids run around the garden.

The menu here goes beyond coffee — one-plate dishes, spaghetti, steak, salads, desserts like crepes, cakes, and bingsu, plus a range of drinks including coffee, tea, Italian soda, smoothies, and homemade bakery items. The must-do is wandering the garden for photos against the white house, ordering a large coffee to sip, then trying a one-plate dish or spaghetti with a dessert. Genuine reviews often praise the atmosphere and the beautifully decorated, shaded setting — ideal for a lazy day off, with both an air-conditioned indoor zone and an outdoor garden seating area.

Costs are light, roughly 101–250 baht per person, with no entry fee — you pay only for food and drink. There's free Wi-Fi, parking, and card payment accepted. Open daily roughly 07:30–18:00; come in the morning or late afternoon when the sun isn't too harsh for better garden photos and a more comfortable outdoor seat.

Worth knowing from genuine reviews: opinions on the food vary somewhat — some praise the dishes, while others say the coffee could be stronger and the bakery quality inconsistent. Service can be slower during busy periods. But the main draw that keeps people coming back is the garden-house atmosphere and photo spots that are hard to find elsewhere on the Phichai side. If you like a garden cafe without driving into downtown Uttaradit, this one delivers.

blocks.text: Uttaradit's attractions are spread across several districts — from Laplae to Sirikit Dam to Ton Sak Yai National Park. If you'd rather not drive yourself or plan the route, booking a guided tour or shuttle makes it easier to cover several spots in one day, and booking tickets in advance via Klook or GetYourGuide cuts down on queueing on-site. blocks.title: Know Before You Go to Uttaradit

items.title: Renting a car is easiest
items.text: Attractions are spread across several districts and Grab is scarce outside town. Renting a car or hiring a car with driver is the most comfortable option. Within town you can walk or use a songthaew, but Sirikit Dam and the giant teak tree require a car.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: The walking street, markets, and most souvenir and local-food stalls mainly take cash. Even though some shops and cafes accept PromptPay QR, keep small bills on hand, especially at the evening market.

items.title: Visit early to avoid sun and crowds
items.text: Outdoor spots like monuments, temples, and the dam crest get hot with little shade. Morning or late afternoon visits are more comfortable and photograph better. Wat Phra Thaen Sila At gets crowded during Makha Bucha, so allow extra time for parking.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Uttaradit sees more Thai visitors than foreign ones, so most signage and menus are in Thai and English speakers are few. Bring a translation app and save place names in Thai script to show drivers.

items.title: Dress modestly at temples
items.text: Wat Phra Thaen Sila At, Wat Don Sak, and the temples in Laplae are genuine places of worship. Dress modestly, cover shoulders and knees, remove your shoes when entering buildings, and handle the old carved wooden doors gently.

items.title: Tipping isn't required
items.text: Restaurants and cafes generally don't require tipping — rounding up or leaving small change is fine. If you hire a car with driver or a guide for a full day, a small tip at the end of the trip is a welcome gesture.

blocks.title: Trip-Planning Tips to Make the Most of Your Day in Uttaradit
blocks.html:
The smoothest route splits into two zones. Day one covers the town and Laplae — start the morning at the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument in front of the provincial hall, then tour the museums behind it. Drive on to Laplae to photograph the city gate and the Widow Monument, visit the Laplae City Museum (free), then pay respects at Wat Phra Thaen Sila At in Thung Yang. Finish at Wat Don Sak to see the Ayutthaya-era carved wooden doors. If it lines up with a weekend evening, head to Uttaradit Walking Street along the irrigation canal right after.

Day two covers nature — drive up to Sirikit Dam in Tha Pla, walk the dam crest or rent a bike to take in the view, then continue to Ton Sak Yai National Park in Nam Pat to see the largest teak tree in the world. If you have time, stop by the Bo Lek Nam Phi iron mines in Thong Saen Khan to try panning for iron as a lucky charm. To close the trip on a relaxed note, CAFE' De FIELD on the Phichai side is a garden cafe for a coffee and photos before heading home. Nature spots get hot with little shade, so go in the morning or late afternoon, and bring water and a hat.

blocks.text: To make the most of an Uttaradit trip, try staying a night so you can visit Wat Phra Thaen Sila At in the morning while it's quiet, then drive up to Sirikit Dam to catch the sunset without rushing back. Popular hotels cluster in downtown Uttaradit, near the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument and the walking street. Pick a location close to whatever you want to see first thing in the morning for the best value — compare prices and reviews before booking.

faq.q: First time in Uttaradit — what shouldn't I miss?
faq.a: The first stop everyone visiting Uttaradit makes is the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument in front of the provincial hall, followed by Laplae with its city gate and Widow Monument, Wat Phra Thaen Sila At Royal Temple in Thung Yang, and if you have time for a longer drive, Sirikit Dam and Ton Sak Yai National Park.

faq.q: What makes Uttaradit's highlights unique compared to elsewhere?
faq.a: Uttaradit holds several 'largest in Thailand/the world' claims — Sirikit Dam is Thailand's largest earthen dam, and Ton Sak Yai National Park is home to the largest teak tree in the world, over a thousand years old. Add in the legend of Laplae, the town of widows, and the Nam Phi steel sword legend at the Bo Lek Nam Phi mines, and you get an experience you won't find in any other province.

Most are free — the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument, Laplae City Gate, Wat Phra Thaen Sila At, Laplae City Museum, Bo Lek Nam Phi iron mines, Wat Don Sak, Sirikit Dam, and the walking street. Ton Sak Yai National Park charges a park fee of 20 baht for adults and 10 baht for children, and Bo Lek Nam Phi only charges if you buy amulets.

Uttaradit's attractions are fairly spread out, so having your own car or a rental is most convenient. In-town spots like the Phraya Phichai Dap Hak Monument and the walking street have easy parking. Laplae is about 5-8 km from downtown, while Sirikit Dam (Tha Pla) and the giant teak tree (Nam Pat) are further out, so allow extra driving time. Major attractions have spacious parking lots.

faq.q: What are the opening hours for Uttaradit's attractions?
faq.a: Most temples and monuments are open daytime through evening — come in the morning for cooler weather and fewer crowds. Museums typically open around 09:00-16:30. Uttaradit Walking Street only runs on weekend evenings, while cafes like CAFE' De FIELD are open daytime through evening. Before visiting specific spots like museums or workshops, check the latest opening hours.
